The war which broke out among ourselves. The Nephites, very often, were the victims of ambitious men who sought only personal office, or places of power, caring little or nothing for God and His children. In Alma 51:13, we read the account of another rebellion which was the cause of Moroni's fears at this time: "And it came to pass that when the men who were called King-Men had heard that the Lamanites were coming down to battle against them, they were glad in their hearts; and they refused to take up arms, for they were so wroth with the Chief Judge, and also with the people of liberty that they would not take up arms to defend their country." Amalickiah was the leader of the King-Men at that time, and in the ensuing battle was defeated by Moroni. Amalickiah then fled to the Lamanites, where by treason and by murder, he worked himself onto their throne. His followers who remained within the borders of the Nephites were compelled to enter a covenant to support the Government of the Republic and the cause of freedom, or be put to death. But few refused to make this covenant, however, great loss of life resulted therefrom much of which being murderings induced by angry passions which were let loose. In his scathing rebuke to Pahoran, Moroni maintained that, beforetime, when peril threatened them as now, contending portions of the people united their strength and supplies, and went against and defeated the common enemy. But, evidently, not so now. The haughty desires of the King-Men had not ceased, and had divided into opposing factions, what should have been a united body politic. They forgot that in unity there is strength.

The Book of Mormon is replete with parallelisms. The poetic patterns serve, as they do in the Bible, to emphasize messages, define and expand them, make them more memorable, and structure them. One form of parallelism, chiasmus, has been extensively studied, but surprisingly, almost nothing has been written on the abundance of other parallelisms in the Book of Mormon. Here is a review of some other types of parallelisms found in the Book of Mormon. Parallelism of numbers. In Hebrew and other Semitic languages, numbers have no synonyms, with the exception of twenty/score. Equivalents in English like twelve/dozen and fractions like half a hundred/fifty do not exist. Numbers are therefore parallel only when they are repeated or given in multiples-the a fortiori, or "how much more so," effect. The Book of Mormon contains both of these types of parallelisms. Only six examples of a fortiori parallelism exist in the Book of Mormon, all using the number tens of thousands in an exaggerated comparison that heightens the sense of multitude, as in Alma 60:22: Yea, will ye sit in idleness while ye are surrounded with thousands of those, yea, and tens of thousands, who do also sit in idleness?
